title: Daily average demand of both datasets
description: Top: average electricity demand of each day for the PJM East region (MW), 2002-2018. Bottom: the same for the UCI household (kW), 2006-2010. It gives a first look at the full data. The region has clear summer and winter peaks every year. The household is much more up and down from day to day and uses most in winter.

title: Example of a wrong value in the PJM data
description: Shows 24 hours of PJM demand around one sudden one-hour jump that is impossible for a whole region. Such points are data errors, so they were replaced by the value between the hour before and the hour after. Real events, like Hurricane Sandy in 2012, were kept.

title: How the longest missing period in the household data was filled
description: Household demand in August 2010, where about 5 days of data are missing. Blue is the original data (with the gap), orange is the data after filling. Short gaps were filled from the neighbouring hours, long gaps with the usual demand for that weekday and hour.

title: Training, validation and test periods
description: Daily average demand coloured by the part of the data it belongs to: training (first 70%, the models learn from it), validation (next 15%, used to choose the model settings) and test (last 15%, used only at the end to measure accuracy). The split is in time order, so the models are always tested on the future.

title: Average demand by hour, weekday and month
description: Left: average demand for each hour of the day, separately for weekdays, weekends and holidays. Middle: average demand for each weekday (0 = Monday). Right: average demand for each month. Top row PJM, bottom row household. The region uses most on weekday afternoons and in summer (air conditioning). The household uses most in the evening, at weekends and in winter.

title: Demand by weekday and hour (heat map)
description: Each square is the average demand for one weekday (rows, 0 = Monday) and one hour of the day (columns). Brighter colour = higher demand. It shows the daily and weekly pattern together: for PJM weekday daytime is brightest, for the household the evenings are brightest.

title: PJM demand split into its parts (MSTL decomposition)
description: The PJM demand is split into four parts: the long-term trend, the daily repeating pattern (24 hours), the weekly repeating pattern (168 hours), and the rest that these patterns cannot explain (residual). A large daily part and a smaller weekly part show that PJM demand repeats strongly every day and every week.

title: Household demand split into its parts (MSTL decomposition)
description: The same split as for PJM, but for the household. The daily and weekly parts are smaller and the rest (residual) is much bigger, so the household demand is much less regular and harder to predict.

title: Daily and weekly patterns over 3 weeks
description: A zoom into the last 3 weeks of the daily and weekly repeating parts from the decomposition. Here you can see the shape of one day and the difference between weekdays and the weekend more clearly than in the full plot.

title: How much demand depends on earlier hours (autocorrelation)
description: Left (ACF): how similar the demand is to the demand 1, 2, ... 200 hours earlier. High bars at 24 and 168 hours mean demand is similar to the same hour yesterday and last week. Right (PACF): the direct link to each earlier hour after removing the effect of the hours in between. PJM depends very strongly on the last hours, the household much less.

title: Which cycles are strongest (periodogram)
description: Shows how strong each repeating cycle is in the data. The red lines mark cycles of 12 hours, 24 hours, 1 week and 1 year. High points mean strong cycles. For PJM the strongest cycles are 24 hours and half a year (summer and winter peaks), then 12 hours and 1 week. For the household the strongest are 12 and 24 hours (morning and evening peaks) and the yearly cycle.

title: When the highest and lowest demand happens
description: Peak = the 10% of hours with the highest demand, low = the 10% with the lowest. Left: in which hours of the day they happen. Right: in which months. PJM peaks are summer afternoons and evenings, lows are spring and autumn nights. Household peaks are winter evenings. These periods are used later to check where the models make bigger errors.

title: Percentage error of the tree models and the simple benchmark
description: Average percentage error (MAPE) on the test period for the seasonal naive benchmark, Random Forest and XGBoost, at 1 hour, 1 day and 1 week ahead. Lower is better. Both tree models are much better than the benchmark, and the error grows the further ahead they predict. Household MAPE looks very high because night demand is close to zero, so small errors become big percentages.

title: Which inputs the tree models use most (1 day ahead)
description: How much each input helps Random Forest and XGBoost when predicting 1 day ahead. Longer bar = more important. For PJM the most important inputs are the demand at the same hour one day before (lag_24) and the hours just after it. For the household the hour of the day and the demand one and two weeks before are most important.

title: Predicted vs actual demand for one test week (tree models)
description: The first week of the test period, predicted 1 day ahead. Black line = actual demand, coloured lines = predictions of the seasonal naive benchmark, Random Forest and XGBoost. Top PJM, bottom household. For PJM the tree models follow the actual demand closely. For the household they follow the usual daily shape but cannot predict the sudden spikes.

title: Error of all seven models
description: Test error (RMSE) of all models at 1 hour, 1 day and 1 week ahead. Lower bar = more accurate. Left PJM (MW), right household (kW). 1 hour ahead the tree models are clearly best. For PJM 1 day and 1 week ahead the neural networks are about as good as the tree models. For the household XGBoost is best at all horizons.

title: Which past hours the attention model looks at
description: For each dataset and horizon: how much weight the attention model gives to each of the last 48 hours before it makes a prediction. If all hours were treated the same, each bar would be about 0.021. The bars are almost equal, so the model does not clearly focus on special hours like the same hour yesterday. The temporal pattern analysis explained the errors better than these weights.

title: Predicted vs actual demand for one test week (all models)
description: The first week of the test period, predicted 1 day ahead. Black line = actual demand, coloured lines = predictions of XGBoost and the four neural networks (LSTM, GRU, CNN-LSTM, attention). Top PJM, bottom household. All models follow the daily shape. Differences are mainly at the peaks, and none of them can predict the sudden household spikes.
